```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Exercises graded on a value instead of the exact code.
# Add an entry here to opt an exercise in, using list(var) to check a variable,
# list(expr) to check a Python expression, or list(last_value = TRUE) to check the
# student's last line. The result is compared against the same thing computed from
# the exercise's -solution chunk; add value = ... to compare against a fixed number
# instead. Add defines = "name" to require the student's code to define that name
# itself. Add structure = c(...) to also require the code to have a certain shape
# (see check_structure below for the rules). Any exercise not listed is graded by
# exact code match against its -solution chunk.
value_checks <- list(
  # Any valid SRS passes: 15 values drawn from sleep_hours without reusing any (checked
  # by comparing value counts), sleep_mean is the mean of the student's own sample, and
  # the code sets replace=False
  srs_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(len(sleep_sample) == 15',
    'and not (__import__("collections").Counter(list(sleep_sample)) - __import__("collections").Counter(list(sleep_hours)))',
    'and bool(np.isclose(sleep_mean, np.mean(sleep_sample))))'),
    value = 1, defines = c("sleep_sample", "sleep_mean"), structure = "no_replace"),
  # Any valid stratified sample passes: 20 different, unchanged rows of dorm, 10 from each
  # year, and the code uses .sample() so the rows are picked at random
  strat_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(len(strat_sample) == 20',
    'and strat_sample.index.is_unique',
    'and bool(strat_sample.index.isin(dorm.index).all())',
    'and bool((strat_sample["year"].value_counts().reindex(["Freshman", "Sophomore"]) == 10).all())',
    'and strat_sample[["year", "sleep_hours"]].equals(dorm.loc[strat_sample.index, ["year", "sleep_hours"]]))'),
    value = 1, defines = "strat_sample", structure = "df_sample"),
  # Any valid cluster sample passes: unchanged rows of dorm_floors making up exactly 2 whole floors
  # (every resident on each chosen floor), and the code picks the floors at random
  cluster_ex = list(expr = paste(
    'int(cluster_sample.index.is_unique',
    'and bool(cluster_sample.index.isin(dorm_floors.index).all())',
    'and cluster_sample["floor"].nunique() == 2',
    'and set(cluster_sample.index) == set(dorm_floors.index[dorm_floors["floor"].isin(cluster_sample["floor"])])',
    'and cluster_sample.equals(dorm_floors.loc[cluster_sample.index]))'),
    value = 1, defines = "cluster_sample", structure = "cluster_random")
)

# Python helpers for custom_checker (done in Python so they work the same on every
# Python version).
# get_result runs code like learnr does (setup objects visible, new variables kept
# separate) and returns the value being checked.
# values_match compares a student's result to the expected one. Data frames and
# series match if they have the same row labels and counts, ignoring their names,
# row order, and the outer level of the column labels (so values = "SID" and
# values = ["SID"] both work).
checker_py <- '
# (imports go inside the functions because py_run_string keeps top-level names local)
def get_result(code, var=None, expr=None, last_value=False, defines=()):
    import ast
    import __main__
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    if last_value:
        if not tree.body:
            raise ValueError("no code")
        last = tree.body[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Assign) and len(last.targets) == 1 and isinstance(last.targets[0], ast.Name):
            # Last line is `name = expr`, so read `name`
            var = last.targets[0].id
        elif isinstance(last, ast.Expr):
            # Rewrite the last line `expr` as `__check_result__ = expr` so we can read it
            target = ast.Name(id="__check_result__", ctx=ast.Store())
            tree.body[-1] = ast.copy_location(ast.Assign(targets=[target], value=last.value), last)
            ast.fix_missing_locations(tree)
            var = "__check_result__"
        else:
            raise ValueError("last line is not an expression")
    user_vars = {}
    exec(compile(tree, "<exercise>", "exec"), __main__.__dict__, user_vars)
    if expr is not None:
        user_vars["__check_result__"] = eval(expr, __main__.__dict__, user_vars)
        var = "__check_result__"
    for name in list(defines) + [var]:
        if name not in user_vars:
            raise NameError(name + " not defined")
    return user_vars[var]

def check_structure(code, rules=()):
    # Returns "" if the code follows every rule, otherwise a message saying what is missing
    import ast
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    nodes = list(ast.walk(tree))
    for rule in rules:
        if rule == "last_eq":
            last = tree.body[-1] if tree.body else None
            value = last.value if isinstance(last, ast.Expr) else None
            if not (isinstance(value, ast.Compare) and len(value.ops) == 1 and isinstance(value.ops[0], ast.Eq)):
                return "Your code should use == to compare the two sides of the Complement Rule."
            if ast.dump(value.left) == ast.dump(value.comparators[0]):
                return "The two sides of your == should be calculated in different ways."
        elif rule == "complement":
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.NotEq) or (isinstance(n, ast.UnaryOp) and isinstance(n.op, ast.Invert)) for n in nodes):
                return "Use a comparison operator like != to find the students who are not in the event."
        elif rule == "arithmetic":
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.BinOp) and isinstance(n.op, (ast.Sub, ast.Add)) for n in nodes):
                return "The Complement Rule relates an event to its complement through subtraction, e.g. 1 - P(not A)."
        elif rule == "no_replace":
            # Needs a random.choice(..., replace=False) call, so a hand-picked sample fails
            calls = [n for n in nodes if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Attribute) and n.func.attr == "choice"]
            if not calls:
                return "Use np.random.choice() to pick the residents at random."
            if not any(k.arg == "replace" and isinstance(k.value, ast.Constant) and k.value.value is False for c in calls for k in c.keywords):
                return "Make sure no resident can be picked more than once (set replace=False)."
        elif rule == "cluster_random":
            calls = [n for n in nodes if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Attribute) and n.func.attr in ("choice", "sample")]
            if not calls:
                return "Use np.random.choice() to pick the floors at random."
            # np.random.choice can pick the same floor twice unless replace=False
            for c in calls:
                if c.func.attr == "choice" and not any(k.arg == "replace" and isinstance(k.value, ast.Constant) and k.value.value is False for k in c.keywords):
                    return "Make sure the same floor cannot be picked twice (set replace=False)."
        elif rule == "df_sample":
            calls = [n for n in nodes if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Attribute) and n.func.attr == "sample"]
            if not calls:
                return "Use .sample() to pick the residents in each year at random."
            # replace=True can pick a resident twice (and sometimes happens not to, so check the code)
            if any(k.arg == "replace" and not (isinstance(k.value, ast.Constant) and k.value.value is False) for c in calls for k in c.keywords):
                return "Make sure no resident can be picked more than once (leave out replace, or set replace=False)."
            # A plain SRS of 20 gets exactly 10 of each year about 1 time in 8, so also
            # require the code to split the residents up by the "year" column
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.Constant) and n.value == "year" for n in nodes):
                return "Use the year column to split the residents into freshmen and sophomores first."
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown structure rule: " + rule)
    return ""

def values_match(actual, expected):
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    if isinstance(expected, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame)):
        actual, expected = [
            x.squeeze(axis=1) if isinstance(x, pd.DataFrame) and x.shape[1] == 1 else x
            for x in (actual, expected)
        ]
        if type(actual) is not type(expected):
            return False
        actual, expected = actual.sort_index(), expected.sort_index()
        if list(actual.index) != list(expected.index):
            return False
        if isinstance(expected, pd.DataFrame):
            last_level = lambda cols: [c[-1] if isinstance(c, tuple) else c for c in cols]
            if last_level(actual.columns) != last_level(expected.columns):
                return False
        try:
            return bool(np.allclose(actual.to_numpy(dtype=float), expected.to_numpy(dtype=float), equal_nan=True))
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            return False
    try:
        return bool(np.isclose(float(actual), float(expected)))
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return False
'

custom_checker <- function(label, user_code, solution_code, check_code, envir_result, evaluate_result, envir_prep, last_value, stage, ...) {
  # (learnr doesn't pass the last value of Python chunks, so we run the code)
  if (label %in% names(value_checks)) {
    if (stage != "check") return()
    spec <- value_checks[[label]]
    structure_msg <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- reticulate::py_run_string(checker_py, local = TRUE, convert = FALSE)
      reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$check_structure(user_code, as.list(spec$structure)))
    }, error = function(e) "")
    if (nzchar(structure_msg)) {
      return(list(message = paste(random_encouragement(), structure_msg), correct = FALSE))
    }
    correct <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- reticulate::py_run_string(checker_py, local = TRUE, convert = FALSE)
      get_result <- function(code) {
        helpers$get_result(code, var = spec$var, expr = spec$expr,
                           last_value = isTRUE(spec$last_value), defines = as.list(spec$defines))
      }
      values_match <- helpers$values_match
      # Student's code runs first, so if it modifies shared data the solution can't fill it in for them
      actual <- get_result(user_code)
      expected <- if (is.null(spec$value)) get_result(solution_code) else reticulate::r_to_py(spec$value)
      isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(values_match(actual, expected)))
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (correct) {
      return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
    }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
  # Exact code checking (requires a <label>-solution chunk and <label>-code-check chunk)
  if (stage == "code_check") {
      if (user_code == solution_code){
          return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
      }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
}

gradethis_setup()
tutorial_options(exercise.completion = FALSE, exercise.checker = custom_checker, exercise.timelimit = 180,
                 exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE
)
```

```{python setup_py, include=FALSE}
study_hours = np.array([17, 35, 16, 20, 23, 24, 28, 22, 27, 12, 23, 21, 16, 20, 13, 16, 22, 17, 15, 12,
                        27, 28, 21, 21, 6, 28, 29, 26, 28, 10, 23, 12, 33, 14, 23, 23, 17, 17, 26, 28,
                        25, 28, 21, 16, 16, 21, 21, 37, 19, 32, 35, 21, 23, 16, 27, 22, 31, 20, 10, 27,
                        25, 21, 16, 25, 25, 28, 13, 35, 25, 23, 32, 30, 2, 24, 12, 24, 9, 22, 27, 25,
                        28, 26, 23, 9, 30, 27, 19, 17, 29, 18, 18, 22, 17, 35, 14, 31, 28, 26, 20, 13])

# Hours of sleep last night for all 60 residents of a dorm house (Simple Random Sampling)
sleep_hours = np.array([6.0, 7.3, 4.7, 8.7, 7.8, 6.6, 6.6, 7.4, 6.7, 6.7, 7.9, 7.6, 6.9, 6.9, 7.2,
                        6.3, 6.5, 7.7, 6.8, 5.4, 6.4, 7.8, 6.7, 6.8, 7.8, 9.2, 6.1, 8.6, 5.5, 7.2,

# The same dorm as a data frame: only freshmen (first 36 rows) and sophomores (last 24) live there
# (Stratified Sampling)
dorm = pd.DataFrame({
    "year": ["Freshman"] * 36 + ["Sophomore"] * 24,
    "sleep_hours": sleep_hours
})

dorm_floors = dorm.assign(floor=list(range(1, 7)) * 6 + list(range(1, 7)) * 4)
```

## Sampling Populations

Throughout this course we have been working with datasets that are *samples* of a larger group---we very rarely have access to the entire population.
In this section we will discuss the differences between populations and samples, and how we might create those samples via different sampling methods.


### Populations vs. Samples

So what is the difference between a population and a sample? A **population** is the entire group of individuals or items that we are interested in studying, while a **sample** is a subset of that population that we actually collect data from.

The numerical characteristics of a population are called **parameters**, while those of a sample are called **statistics**. For example, the average height of all adults in the United States is a population parameter, while the average height of a sample of 100 adults is a sample statistic. See the table below for some common measures and their corresponding population parameters and sample statistics.

::: {.disttable .stattable}
| Measure | Population Parameter | Sample Statistic | Use |
|:----------|:----------:|:----------:|:------------------------------|
| Mean | $\mu$ | $\bar{x}$ | Measuring the center/location of a distribution |
| Standard Deviation | $\sigma$ | $s$ | Measuring the spread/scale of a distribution |
| Proportion | $\pi$ or $p$ | $p$ or $\hat{p}$ | Measuring the frequency of a binary variable |
:::

Suppose researchers at the University of Chicago want to know how many hours per week its undergraduates spend studying. To find out, a researcher goes to Regenstein Library at 10pm on a Tuesday and surveys 100 students about how many hours they study per week.

```{r q1, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "What is the population in this scenario?",
  answer("All undergraduates at UChicago", correct = TRUE),
  answer("The 100 students who were surveyed in Regenstein", message = "These are the students we actually collected data from. Is that the whole group the researchers want to learn about?"),
  answer("All students who were in Regenstein at 10pm on Tuesday", message = "The researchers want to learn about all UChicago undergraduates, not just the ones in Regenstein that night."),
  answer("The average number of hours UChicago undergraduates study per week", message = "This is a number describing the group, not the group itself."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

```{r q2, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "What is the sample in this scenario?",
  answer("The 100 students who were surveyed in Regenstein", correct = TRUE),
  answer("All undergraduates at UChicago", message = "This is the whole group the researchers want to learn about. Did we collect data from all of them?"),
  answer("All students who were in Regenstein at 10pm on Tuesday", message = "Only the 100 students who were surveyed gave us data."),
  answer("The average number of hours studied per week among the students surveyed in Regenstein", message = "This is a number calculated from the group we collected data from, not the group itself."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

### Sampling Methods

In order to use the sample to make plausible claim about the population, we need to make sure that the sample is representative of the population. There are several different sampling methods that can be used to achieve this, which we will review in this section.

#### Simple Random Sampling 

With this sampling method, every individual in the population has an equal chance of being selected for the sample. In practice, this can be achieved by using a random number generator or drawing names from a hat. We can implement Simple Random Sampling easily in Python using the `numpy` function `np.random.choice()`. 

For this example, let's imagine that our 100 student array `study_hours` is our *population* of interest, i.e., we only care about the 100 students who were studying in Regenstein at 10 pm on a particular Tuesday night. 
We can use the following code to take a simple random sample of 10 students from the `study_hours` array:

```{python srs-example, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Randomly pick 10 students; replace=False means no student can be picked twice
srs_sample = np.random.choice(study_hours, size=10, replace=False)

print(srs_sample)
print(np.mean(srs_sample))
```

Notice that if you run the code repeatedly, the sample and mean will change each time. This is because each student is equally likely to be selected, so the sample is random.

```{r q6, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "True or False: Choosing a random starting student and then taking every 10th student in `study_hours` after them is a simple random sample.",
  answer("True", message = "Every student does have the same 1 in 10 chance of being picked, but that isn't enough. Try again."),
  answer("False", correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Every sample of 10 students is not equally likely: two students who are next to each other in the array can never be in the same sample. This method is called systematic sampling."),
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

#### Stratified Sampling 

With a stratified sample, the population is divided into subgroups (strata) based on certain characteristics, and a random sample is taken from each stratum. This ensures that the sample is representative of the population with respect to those characteristics.

Let's go back to the dorm from the previous question. Assume only freshmen and sophomores live in this dorm. Because students in different years might have different sleep habits, we want our sample to include the same number of students from each year. 

The data frame `dorm` contains the same 60 residents as `sleep_hours`, with a `year` column that says whether each resident is a `"Freshman"` or a `"Sophomore"`, and a `sleep_hours` column with the hours of sleep they got last night. Here are the first few rows:

```{python dorm-head, exercise = TRUE, exercise.eval = FALSE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
dorm.head()
```

Using the code template below, take a stratified sample of 10 freshmen and 10 sophomores from `dorm`, and save it as `strat_sample`.

```{python strat_ex, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Split the population into strata (separate data frames)
freshmen = ......
sophomores = ......

# Take a simple random sample from each stratum
fresh_sample = freshmen.sample(...)
soph_sample = sophomores.sample(...)

# Combine the samples
strat_sample = pd.concat([fresh_sample, soph_sample])

```

```{python strat_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Split the population into strata
freshmen = dorm[dorm["year"] == "Freshman"]
sophomores = dorm[dorm["year"] == "Sophomore"]

# Take a simple random sample from each stratum
fresh_sample = freshmen.sample(n=10)
soph_sample = sophomores.sample(n=10)

# Combine the samples
strat_sample = pd.concat([fresh_sample, soph_sample])
```

#### Cluster Sampling

The population is divided into clusters (often based on geography or other natural groupings), and a random sample of clusters is selected. All individuals within the selected clusters are then included in the sample.

Let's go back to our dorm. The dorm has 6 floors, numbered 1 through 6, and 10 residents live on each floor. Instead of tracking down individual residents all over the building, we could randomly choose 2 floors and survey *every* resident on those floors. Here, each floor is a cluster.

The data frame `dorm_floors` contains the same residents as `dorm`, plus a `floor` column that says which floor each resident lives on. Using the code template below, randomly choose 2 of the 6 floors, then save every resident who lives on one of those floors as `cluster_sample`. The `pandas` method `.isin()` will be helpful here: `df["col"].isin(value_list)` is `True` for each row whose value in `"col"` is in `value_list`.

```{python cluster_ex, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup="setup_py"}
# Randomly choose 2 of the 6 floors (the clusters)
chosen_floors = np.random.choice(......)

# Keep every resident who lives on one of the chosen floors
cluster_sample = dorm_floors[......]

```

```{python cluster_ex-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# Randomly choose 2 of the 6 floors (the clusters)
chosen_floors = np.random.choice([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], size=2, replace=False)

# Keep every resident who lives on one of the chosen floors
cluster_sample = dorm_floors[dorm_floors["floor"].isin(chosen_floors)]
```

```{r cluster_ex-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```


Note that **multistage sampling** is a combination of the above methods, where the population is divided into clusters, and then a random sample of individuals is taken from each selected cluster.

#### Convenience Sampling

The sample is selected based on ease of access or availability, rather than random selection. This method is often used in practice, but it can lead to biased samples that are not representative of the population.

```{r q9, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "Researchers want to learn some information about all UChicago undergraduates. Which of the following are convenience samples? Select all that apply.",
  answer("Surveying the first 50 students who walk into Regenstein on a Monday morning", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Surveying every student eating lunch in the dining hall closest to the researchers' office", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Asking the 30 students in the researchers' own DATA 118 section to fill out the survey", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Randomly drawing 50 student IDs from the registrar's list of all undergraduates", message = "Every undergraduate has an equal chance of being picked here, so this is a simple random sample."),
  answer("Randomly selecting 20 students from each class year", message = "This takes a random sample from each group, so it is a stratified sample."),
  answer("Randomly choosing 5 houses and surveying every resident in them", message = "This randomly picks whole groups and surveys everyone in them, so it is a cluster sample."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```

### Bias

We must be careful about how we sample populations. Without care, several kinds of bias can arise, including **selection bias**, **non-response bias**, **response bias**, **survivorship bias**, and **undercoverage bias**. You can read more about each of these [here](https://ds1.datascience.uchicago.edu/09/4/biases.html). Once you've done that, answer the following question.

```{r q10, echo=FALSE}
question(
  "To learn how much UChicago undergraduates study, researchers email a survey to every undergraduate. Many students with the heaviest course loads are too busy to fill it out, so most of the responses come from students with lighter schedules. Which kind of bias does this survey suffer from?",
  answer("Non-response bias", correct = TRUE, message = "The students who didn't respond are different in a meaningful way (they study more) from the students who did."),
  answer("Response bias", message = "Response bias is about the answers people give being inaccurate, like underreporting embarrassing behavior. Here, the problem is who didn't answer at all."),
  answer("Survivorship bias"),
  answer("Undercoverage bias", message = "Undercoverage bias happens when some groups are left out of who gets surveyed. Here, every undergraduate was sent the survey."),
  allow_retry = TRUE,
  random_answer_order = TRUE
)
```
